sb_prompt: PLEASE DISCUSS CARE OF THE ELDERLY.  FIND OUT HOW THE OTHER CALLER FEELS ABOUT SENDING AN ELDERLY FAMILY MEMBER TO A NURSING HOME.  WHAT SHOULD ONE KNOW ABOUT THE NURSING HOME ENVIRONMENT WHEN MAKING THIS DECISION?
turns: So, um, why did you call? I was supposed to ask about nursing homes, but honestly... I've thought about putting my own mom there for years. I mean, part of me thinks it's the only way to keep her safe, but another part just feels like giving up. I guess I never really figured out which side was right until recently.

Yeah, I get that feeling, honestly. My dad had a stroke a few years back and we ended up putting him in a facility. It was... well, it wasn't pretty at first. There was a lot of crying in the lobby and the staff seemed really overwhelmed. But then, you know, about three weeks in, he actually started laughing at a joke a volunteer told him, and I realized he was safe. Like, nobody was falling in the bathroom anymore. So I guess my point is, maybe it's not about giving up, it's just about knowing when you're not strong enough to keep them safe themselves?

Yeah, three weeks in? That's... that's actually pretty fast to adjust to it. I mean, I guess I never thought of it as "giving up" until I heard you say that, because if she gets hurt at home, that's definitely giving up on her safety too. But I still worry about the boredom, you know? Like, if she just sits in a chair all day with nobody to talk to her, does that feel like giving up? And you said the staff was overwhelmed at first, did they get better with your dad?

Yeah, they got better pretty quick. The director came in and actually changed the whole schedule, made sure there were more activities and stuff, so it's totally different now. My dad's in his own little room now and he's actually got friends again, which is weird because I thought it'd be lonely or something.

That's actually kinda surprising, honestly, because I heard stories like that from other families who said it was just a bunch of people staring at walls all day, but I guess maybe those places just needed someone to step up?

Yeah, and honestly that director thing is kinda wild because I didn't even know it was a choice until I heard about it, but I guess that's the thing you gotta know before you decide—like, you can't just pick any place, you gotta ask if they actually have activities or if it's just gonna be a wait for death.

Wait, so you're saying it's not automatic? I've been assuming that once you call the director, they're just gonna follow a checklist and nobody has to do anything special. That's the part I'm stuck on. If I don't actually have to fight to get her safe, then maybe my hesitation is just... pride? Or maybe I'm just scared of the work involved? Because honestly, if I have to lobby the place to make sure she's not just sitting in a chair staring at a wall, that sounds exhausting. What if we pick a place that doesn't do that?

Yeah, exactly, that's the worst part, you don't even know until you visit, like you can't just assume everyone gets taken care of unless you actually go in there and ask to see the daily schedule and ask the staff what they do when the patient isn't awake or napping.

Yeah, that's the scary part, asking them specifically about the non-nap hours, because if they just say "we have bingo twice a week" but the staff never actually check on the folks in between... that's when you start wondering if they're lying or just don't care.

Yeah, that's the part that bugs me the most—like, how do you tell if they're actually checking or just going through the motions? Because sometimes the answer sounds real enough, but then you realize they're not actually doing anything between bingo.

Yeah, but it's just that scary because if you ask them and they say "our staff checks every two hours," how do you know if they mean it or if they're just saying that to get you to sign the contract? I mean, what if the answer is real but then you find out they're not actually doing it?

Exactly, because usually they'll give you that perfect little staff answer that sounds real, but then you see your family member sitting in the same chair for six hours and you realize they literally weren't even there to check.
That's the thing that just makes me feel like I'm signing away her life, right? Because if they're not really checking, who's watching her if I can't go down there?

Yeah, it's wild because usually the nurse won't even admit that they weren't there, they'll just tell you the logs are perfect, but you gotta actually watch the room for a few hours to see if the person's actually moving or just staring at the same spot like a statue.

That's a nightmare, though. If I have to sit in there for six hours just watching her like a statue... I don't even want to think about getting on a camera or sitting in the lobby all day just to make sure they're actually touching her. I feel like if I do that, I'm just the crazy kid who can't trust anyone, but if I don't, she's just sitting there forgotten. I'm totally lost on what to do.
Yeah, but you know, if you just sit there all day, isn't it actually worse than the risk at home? Like, isn't sitting there forgotten kind of the same as a fall?
That's a good point though, because honestly if I'm watching her all day she's just going to be scared of me, which is worse than anyone ignoring her.
Yeah, but then again, if she's scared of you, maybe you should just visit less so she can have some peace, right?
Yeah, but if I visit less, I don't know if she's actually being checked on, and if I'm there and she's scared, I feel like I'm poisoning the well before I even start.

That's the thing though, if you're there all the time, you're the only one she sees, so if she falls when you're gone, nobody's there to help her, but if you're there, you're just a shadow that makes her feel worse than the lonely chair ever did.
Yeah, but if you don't go in there, how do you even know if you're poisoning the well or if she's actually safe?

Exactly, because you can't tell unless you look for the signs yourself, like if the staff just walk by without making eye contact or if the resident looks like they've forgotten how to stand up on their own.
That's the thing, though, I don't know how to look for those signs without just making her feel like I'm inspecting her like a product.
You can see if her face looks kind of stuck or if she's actually responding to the nurses when they come in.

Yeah, but that's the problem, isn't it? Because if I'm watching her face and she looks stuck, I'm just proving my worst fear to myself, which is worse than just trusting the staff and letting them do their job.

Yeah, but maybe you just ask the family in the room what they actually see instead of asking the manager, because sometimes the manager knows all the rules but the family knows who's actually watching versus who just walks by.

Yeah, that's actually the scariest part, asking the other people in the room instead of the manager, because if I ask my mom "are you safe" she's probably just gonna say "yes" even if she isn't, and then I'm just hearing what I want to hear while the logs lie.

Yeah, that's the thing though, because usually the answer from the other families is just "she's fine," and then you find out two days later that she's been staring at the same tile for six hours and they never even touched her leg to check the skin.

Yeah, that's the worst part because if she says she's fine, how do I know she's not just agreeing because she's scared of what I'll hear? I feel like I'm either gonna be the bad kid who can't trust anyone or the bad kid who trusts too much.

Yeah, but maybe you just ask the family in the room what they actually see instead of asking the manager, because sometimes the manager knows all the rules but the family knows who's actually watching versus who just walks by.
Yeah but if I ask her she'll just smile and say "yes" even if her leg's got that red spot and she's been sitting there for hours, so how do I know she's lying to me or just scared of what I'll find?

Yeah, but maybe you just don't ask her if she's okay, you just ask the nurse if they've logged the check and if the skin actually looks clear, because if the staff aren't honest, nobody's gonna tell the mom the truth anyway.
Yeah, but if the nurse just says "log is clear" without even looking at her skin, how do I know they're lying to you or just reading it off a clipboard without caring?

Yeah, that's the thing though, you can't just trust the clipboard, because if the nurse doesn't actually look at the skin, the log just looks perfect even when the resident's got a deep bruise they never reported.
So if they just look at the clipboard and don't actually touch her skin, isn't that basically the same as never checking her at all?
Yeah, that's the thing though, if they aren't actually touching her, the whole log is just a piece of paper nobody believes, so you're basically left with nothing but your own hope.
So if the log is a lie, does that mean I'm just supposed to hope my mom isn't sitting on a bruised leg for six hours while I'm at the store?
Yeah, but you can't hope your way out of a physical injury, you gotta see the bruises for yourself before you sign that paper.
Yeah, but if I can't see the bruises for myself, then what am I supposed to do? Just guess?
Yeah, but you gotta find a place that lets you come in whenever you want, not just once a week, because that's the only way you actually see if the bruises are real or not.
